question: What does the word 'palsy' mean in relation to cerebral palsy?
explanation: Palsy specifically refers to a lack of muscle control or weakness that interferes with normal movement. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is cerebral palsy described as a non-progressive condition?

options.A: Symptoms always improve steadily without any medical care
options.B: Treatment can completely repair the damaged brain tissue
options.C: The original brain injury does not get worse over time
options.D: The child will eventually outgrow all physical symptoms

explanation: While the physical body changes and challenges may evolve as a child grows, the underlying brain damage remains static. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which infant condition involves high bilirubin levels that can cause brain damage and lead to cerebral palsy?
explanation: Kernicterus occurs when severe neonatal jaundice goes untreated, allowing bilirubin to cross into the brain and cause permanent injury. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h2)

question: Why are very premature babies with low birth weight at a higher risk of developing cerebral palsy?

options.A: Fragile blood vessels in the immature brain easily rupture and bleed
options.B: Premature babies automatically have defective muscle tissue from birth
options.C: The lungs fail to develop, which immediately starves the heart of oxygen
options.D: Infant formulas lack the essential fats required for nerve growth

explanation: Preterm babies have very delicate blood vessels in their brains that can easily bleed, which can damage the surrounding brain tissue. Great insight for your clinical postings! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h2)

question: Damage to which part of the brain is primarily responsible for the balance and coordination problems seen in ataxic cerebral palsy?
explanation: The cerebellum is the main brain structure that regulates balance, posture, and coordinated movement. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h3)

question: A child with cerebral palsy presents with very stiff muscles and hyperactive reflexes. Which type of cerebral palsy is this child most likely experiencing?
explanation: Spastic cerebral palsy is marked by increased muscle tone and exaggerated reflexes because of injury to the motor cortex or pyramidal tracts. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h3)

question: At what age might a nurse suspect a motor issue if an infant consistently prefers using only one hand?
explanation: Babies usually don't show a strong hand preference early on. Showing one-sided preference before 18 months can be an early sign of hemiplegic cerebral palsy. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h4)

question: A 10-month-old cannot sit unsupported, keeps fists clenched, and has stiff legs that cross like scissors when lifted. What should you suspect?
explanation: Delayed sitting, tight fists, and scissoring legs are classic signs that point towards cerebral palsy during developmental checks. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which diagnostic imaging tool is most commonly used to identify structural brain abnormalities in a child with suspected cerebral palsy?
explanation: An MRI provides detailed images of brain tissue, helping clinicians identify areas of past injury or malformation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h5)

question: Why are regular developmental check-ups by a nurse so important during a baby's first year?

options.A: It replaces the need for any laboratory blood tests or physical examinations
options.B: It proves whether the parents caused the infant's developmental injuries
options.C: It accurately predicts the exact adult height the child will eventually reach
options.D: It helps catch early signs of neurological delays so interventions can start promptly

explanation: Catching delays early lets therapy start when a baby's brain is still developing rapidly and can adapt best! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h5)

question: Which healthcare professional primarily helps a child with cerebral palsy learn how to perform daily living tasks like eating and dressing independently?
explanation: Occupational therapists specialize in helping patients develop fine motor skills needed for everyday activities and self-care. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is a major goal of physical therapy in the long-term management of a child with spastic cerebral palsy?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any assistive devices by age five
options.B: Preventing joint contractures and improving functional mobility
options.C: Permanently stopping all involuntary muscle contractions
options.D: Curing the underlying brain lesion through intense exercise

explanation: Physical therapy uses stretching, strengthening, and positioning to keep muscles pliable and prevent permanent joint tightening. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of recommending respite care to a family caring for a child with severe cerebral palsy?

options.A: To give primary caregivers temporary relief from daily caregiving duties
options.B: To permanently transfer legal custody of the child to the hospital
options.C: To teach the child how to live independently in an apartment
options.D: To provide intensive physical therapy without the parents present

explanation: Respite care gives parents a much-needed break to rest and recharge, helping prevent caregiver burnout. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h7)

question: Why should nurses check on the emotional well-being of brothers and sisters in a family affected by cerebral palsy?

options.A: Parents usually ignore the affected child to focus entirely on healthy siblings
options.B: Siblings must legally take over financial caregiving once they turn eighteen
options.C: Siblings are at high risk of developing cerebral palsy themselves
options.D: Siblings can experience feelings of neglect, stress, or added responsibilities

explanation: A chronic condition affects the whole household. Siblings often need emotional support to handle changing roles and big feelings. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common long-term musculoskeletal complication associated with cerebral palsy?
explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune joint disease, not a musculoskeletal complication caused by chronic muscle imbalance from cerebral palsy. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h8)

question: What mainly determines whether a person with cerebral palsy will live independently as an adult?

options.A: The severity of the physical impairment and presence of associated cognitive or communication deficits
options.B: The specific month of the year that the original brain injury took place
options.C: The total number of siblings living in the same household
options.D: Whether the infant received physical therapy before turning six months old

explanation: How much independence a person achieves depends mostly on how severely their movement, thinking, and communication are affected by the injury. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h8)
